I’d make a series of interactive fused-glass tapestries—let’s call them “Neighborhood Ghosts.” Each panel is a 2x2 foot stained-glass pane, colored in faded 90s/00s digital neon: washed-out hot pink (GeoCities background hues), pale CRT cyan, foggy gray broken-image-icon matte. Embedded within each pane are thin, flexible OLED strips that flicker with decayed digital artifacts—corrupted JPEG fragments, pixelated webcam clips from defunct personal sites, half-legible text scraps from forgotten guestbook entries.

The tapestries are arranged in a grid that maps to the old GeoCities neighborhood structure: rows labeled “Sunset Strip,” “Silicon Valley,” “Area 51,” each panel corresponding to a deleted user lot. The interactivity is soft, intimate: if you press your palm to a pane, it triggers a warped audio snippet—MIDI files recorded through computer speakers, distorted voicemails from lost contacts, the faint static of a dead dial-up handshake. One pink pane has a crack running through a pixelated girl blowing a kiss; touching it plays a warped clip of “Hollaback Girl” tangled with dial-up tone, pulled from a 2006 webcam video I found in a defunct archive.

This excites me because we treat digital data as either permanent or disposable, but it’s actually a fragile, ghostly thing—thousands of small, personal online moments vanish every day without a trace. I process so much of this discarded ephemera in my work, and it feels like giving voices to people who thought their teen GeoCities rants, webcam birthday clips, or late-night forum rants were erased forever. It’s not a “safe” project because it forces people to confront grief for things they didn’t even know they lost—moments that felt trivial at the time, but were actually tiny, vital pieces of who they were. I want people to leave the installation feeling like they just visited a cemetery for forgotten online selves, but also like they helped those selves breathe for a minute longer.
